strengths: The motivating counterexample clearly demonstrates why selecting intervention scopes matters: conditioning decisions on context can outperform both unconditional interventions and jointly controlling every actionable variable. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b06/review-experiment-g_1hyc4z/call-98252dad761849d7822109f5e82c99cd/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
Combining existing possibly optimal mixed policy scope (POMPS) theory with contextual Bayesian optimisation is a sensible approach to exploiting causal structure in continuous decision problems.

The experiments report 110 seeds and uncertainty intervals, examine settings where baselines can and cannot attain the optimum, and acknowledge the additional search cost when ordinary contextual BO already performs well.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited. POMPS identification comes from prior work, the optimisation backend is HEBO, and scope selection uses standard UCB. The paper does not provide a sufficiently strong new analysis or broad empirical result to establish the significance of this integration.

The UCB justification in Section 4.2 is incomplete. Each arm's reward distribution changes as its underlying policy learns, so standard stationary-bandit confidence arguments do not directly apply. Stating that rewards become stationary at optimality does not establish convergence to that optimum. Decreasing average-regret curves over 700 iterations are consistent with improvement but do not establish asymptotically sublinear regret.

The general mixed-policy formulation is not adequately connected to the implemented optimiser. Definitions 3.1–3.2 allow different information sets for different actions, whereas Section 4 jointly optimises all actions given an aggregated context. The paper does not explain how this respects individual information constraints or handles contexts observed after earlier interventions. The experiments do not test these more general scopes.

The experiments do not isolate the proposed selector's contribution. In both CaBO comparisons, CoCa-BO has only one POMPS, so its improved performance cannot demonstrate a benefit from UCB selection. Comparisons using identical scopes and optimisation backends with random, round-robin, or alternative acquisition-based selection are missing.

Evaluation is confined to constructed SCMs with only one or two candidate POMPSes. Appendix C adds many redundant variables but still has two scopes, leaving scalability in the number of candidate scopes untested. There are no runtime measurements, broader application benchmarks, or comparisons with the cited mixed-policy reinforcement-learning method in an overlapping discrete setting.

Reproducibility is weakened by material specification errors and missing details. Appendix A.2 omits Cancer from the printed PSA equation, although the subsequent optimality derivation requires that term; Appendix C specifies the self-dependent equation C4 ~ N(C4, 0.1). These may be transcription errors, but they make the implemented benchmarks and oracle objectives ambiguous. UCB settings, baseline configurations, and several intervention domains are also insufficiently specified, and the manuscript provides no identifiable link to the claimed code release.
